question: A 45-year-old woman with chronic IDA has Hb 6.2 g/dL but is haemodynamically stable, tolerating her symptoms (mild fatigue, no dyspnoea at rest). She has no cardiac disease. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?

answers.text: Packed red cell transfusion — transfuse 2 units immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transfusion at Hb 6.2 g/dL in a haemodynamically stable, asymptomatic (at rest) patient with chronic anaemia is not automatically indicated. Chronic anaemia allows physiological adaptation. WHO/NICE guidelines suggest transfusion threshold of Hb < 7 g/dL for stable patients, or < 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease — but stability and symptoms must guide the decision.

answers.text: Oral iron therapy with close monitoring and follow-up in 4 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For haemodynamically stable chronic IDA with mild symptoms, oral iron is first-line. Chronic anaemia causes physiological compensation (increased 2,3-DPG, cardiac output adaptation). Transfusion is reserved for Hb < 7 g/dL with symptoms, haemodynamic instability, or when rapid correction is needed (surgery, near-term pregnancy).

IV iron is indicated when oral iron fails (malabsorption, intolerance, inflammatory bowel disease) or rapid correction is needed (late pregnancy, pre-operative). It is not first-line for a stable ambulatory patient who can absorb oral iron.

Erythropoietin is indicated for anaemia of chronic kidney disease or chemotherapy-induced anaemia, not for IDA. Giving EPO in IDA would not help if iron stores are depleted — EPO requires adequate iron to stimulate erythropoiesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Transfusion is life-saving in acute haemorrhage or symptomatic severe anaemia (Hb < 7 with dyspnoea/cardiac strain). For chronic stable IDA with mild symptoms, cause-directed oral iron therapy is safer, cheaper, and avoids transfusion risks (alloimmunisation, infection, TACO).
Correct. Stable chronic IDA with mild symptoms → oral iron. Transfusion threshold for stable adults is generally Hb < 7 g/dL (lower threshold for young, otherwise healthy patients).
